{{short description|Service that attempts to obscure cryptocurrency money trails}}
A '''cryptocurrency tumbler''' or '''cryptocurrency mixing service'''<ref>{{cite news|last1=Jeffries|first1=Adrianne|title=How to steal Bitcoin in three easy steps|url=https://www.theverge.com/2013/12/19/5183356/how-to-steal-bitcoin-in-three-easy-steps|access-date=17 May 2015|date=19 December 2013|archive-date=10 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210510195348/https://www.theverge.com/2013/12/19/5183356/how-to-steal-bitcoin-in-three-easy-steps|url-status=live}}</ref> is a service that mixes potentially identifiable or "tainted" [[cryptocurrency]] funds with others, so as to obscure the trail back to the fund's original source.<ref>[https://ssrn.com/abstract=3080361 The Cryptocurrency Tumblers: Risks, Legality and Oversight.] Law and Society: Private Law - Financial Law Journal. Social Science Research Network (SSRN). Accessed 6 December 2017.</ref> This is usually done by pooling together source funds from multiple inputs for a large and random period of time, and then spitting them back out to destination addresses. As all the funds are lumped together and then distributed at random times, it is very difficult to trace exact coins. Tumblers have arisen to improve the [[anonymity]] of cryptocurrencies, usually [[bitcoin]] (hence '''bitcoin mixer'''), since the digital currencies provide a public [[ledger]] of all transactions. Due to its goal of anonymity, tumblers have been used to [[Money laundering|money launder]] cryptocurrency.

== Background ==
Tumblers take a percentage [[transaction fee]] of the total coins mixed to turn a profit, typically 1–3%.<ref name="laundry"/> Mixing helps protect privacy and can also be used for [[money laundering]] by mixing illegally obtained funds. Mixing large amounts of money may be illegal, being in violation of [[anti-structuring law]]s. [[Financial crimes]] author [[Jeffrey Robinson]] has suggested tumblers should be criminalized due to their potential use in illegal activities, specifically funding [[terrorism]];<ref name="laundry">{{cite news|last1=Allison|first1=Ian|title=Bitcoin tumbler: The business of covering tracks in the world of cryptocurrency laundering|url=http://www.ibtimes.co.uk/bitcoin-tumbler-business-covering-tracks-world-cryptocurrency-laundering-1487480|access-date=17 May 2015|date=February 11, 2015|archive-date=24 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924045528/http://www.ibtimes.co.uk/bitcoin-tumbler-business-covering-tracks-world-cryptocurrency-laundering-1487480|url-status=live}}</ref> however, a report from the [[Combating Terrorism Center|CTC]] suggests such use in terrorism-related activities is "relatively limited".<ref>{{cite news|last1=Brantly|first1=Aaron|title=Financing Terror Bit by Bit|url=https://www.ctc.usma.edu/posts/financing-terror-bit-by-bit|access-date=17 May 2015|date=31 October 2014|archive-date=23 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170523235646/https://www.ctc.usma.edu/posts/financing-terror-bit-by-bit|url-status=dead}}</ref> There has been at least one incident where an [[Digital currency exchanger|exchange]] has blacklisted "tainted" deposits descending from stolen bitcoins.<ref>{{cite web |last=ICIJ |first= |title=Binance, exchanges moved dirty crypto after crackdown |url=https://www.icij.org/investigations/coin-laundry/cryptocurrency-exchanges-binance-okx-money-laundering-crime/ |publisher=International Consortium of Investigative Journalists |accessdate=20 November 2025}}</ref>

The existence of tumblers has made the anonymous use of [[darknet market]]s easier and the job of law enforcement harder.<ref name="jane">{{cite news|last1=IHS Jane's Intelligence Review|title=Law enforcement struggles to control darknet|url=http://www.janes.com/article/47455/law-enforcement-struggles-to-control-darknet|access-date=6 July 2015|date=30 December 2014|archive-date=17 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150917074919/http://www.janes.com/article/47455/law-enforcement-struggles-to-control-darknet|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Peer-to-peer tumblers ==
[[Peer-to-peer]] tumblers act as a place of meeting for bitcoin users, instead of taking bitcoins for mixing. Users arrange mixing by themselves. This model solves the problem of stealing, as there is no middleman. When it is completely formed, the exchange of bitcoins between the participants begins. Apart from mixing server, none of the participants can know the connection between the incoming and outgoing addresses of coins.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=See|first1=Kenneth|title=The Satoshi laundromat: a review on the money laundering open door of Bitcoin mixers|journal=Journal of Financial Crime|doi=10.1108/JFC-11-2022-0269|date=2023|volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=416–426 }}</ref>

== Money laundering ==
In December 2013, cryptocurrency tumbler Bitcoin Fog<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.wired.com/story/bitcoin-fog-dark-web-cryptocurrency-arrest/ |title=Bitcoin Fog |magazine=Wired |last1=Greenberg |first1=Andy |access-date=2021-05-03 |archive-date=2021-12-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211218202411/https://www.wired.com/story/bitcoin-fog-dark-web-cryptocurrency-arrest/ |url-status=live }}</ref> was used to launder a part of the 96,000 [[Bitcoin|BTC]] from the robbery of [[Sheep Marketplace]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Edwards|first1=Jim|title=A Thief Is Attempting To Hide $US100 Million In Stolen Bitcoins -- And You Can Watch It Live Right Now|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/a-thief-is-attempting-to-hide-100-million-in-stolen-bitcoins-and-you-can-watch-it-live-right-now-2013-12|access-date=17 May 2015|date=4 Dec 2013|archive-date=29 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211229152048/https://www.businessinsider.com.au/a-thief-is-attempting-to-hide-100-million-in-stolen-bitcoins-and-you-can-watch-it-live-right-now-2013-12|url-status=live}}</ref> 

In February 2015, a total of 7,170 Bitcoin was stolen from the Chinese [[Digital currency exchanger|exchange]] Bter.com and traced back to the same tumbler.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Ghoshal|first1=Abhimanyu|title=Chinese Bitcoin exchange Bter will pay back users after losing $1.75 million in cyberattack|url=https://thenextweb.com/insider/2015/03/12/chinese-bitcoin-exchange-bter-will-pay-back-users-after-losing-1-75-million-in-cyberattack/|publisher=The Next Web|access-date=9 September 2015|date=12 March 2015|archive-date=8 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201108135025/http://thenextweb.com/insider/2015/03/12/chinese-bitcoin-exchange-bter-will-pay-back-users-after-losing-1-75-million-in-cyberattack/|url-status=live}}</ref> 

In May 2019, [[FinCEN]] published a Guidance document that mentioned anonymizing services and mentioned particularly "tumblers".<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/2019-05/FinCEN%20Guidance%20CVC%20FINAL%20508.pdf |title=Application of FinCEN's Regulations to Certain Business Models Involving Convertible Virtual Currencies |access-date=2022-08-18 |archive-date=2021-11-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211116144139/https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/2019-05/FinCEN%20Guidance%20CVC%20FINAL%20508.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

In February 2020, the alleged operator of a cryptocurrency tumbler was indicted on charges of "money laundering conspiracy, operating an unlicensed money transmitting business and conducting money transmission without a D.C. license."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/ohio-resident-charged-operating-darknet-based-bitcoin-mixer-which-laundered-over-300-million|title=Ohio Resident Charged with Operating Darknet-Based Bitcoin "Mixer," which Laundered Over $300 Million|date=2020-02-13|website=www.justice.gov|language=en|access-date=2020-02-17|archive-date=2022-05-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220512040537/https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/ohio-resident-charged-operating-darknet-based-bitcoin-mixer-which-laundered-over-300-million|url-status=live}}</ref>

In January 2021, the Department of Justice conducted an operation targeting the ransomware hacker NetWalker, successfully confiscating around $500,000 in digital assets. Then, in February 2021, they apprehended three hackers affiliated with the North Korean military, recovering $2 million in illicitly acquired digital assets.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hossain |first=Mohammad Belayet |date=2023-11-28 |title=Acquiring an awareness of the latest regulatory developments concerning digital assets and anti-money laundering |url=https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/JMLC-10-2022-0147/full/html |journal=Journal of Money Laundering Control |language=en |volume=26 |issue=6 |pages=1261–1268 |doi=10.1108/JMLC-10-2022-0147 |issn=1368-5201 |access-date=2024-04-11 |archive-date=2023-11-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231126042925/https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/JMLC-10-2022-0147/full/html |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{Relevance inline|paragraph|date=May 2026|reason=It's not clear from this paragraph how it's related to cryptocurrency tumblers. Clarify that connection or remove the paragraph.}}

In April 2021, U.S. Federal authorities arrested the founder of Bitcoin Fog, a Russian-Swedish man named Roman Sterlingov, on charges of money laundering, operating an unlicensed money transmitting business, and money transmission without a license in the District of Columbia. It was alleged that during its 10 years of operation, Bitcoin Fog laundered over 1.2 million [[Bitcoin]] at a value of approximately $335 million.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Lyons|first=Kim|date=2021-04-29|title=Feds arrest founder of bitcoin 'mixer' they say laundered $335 million over ten years|url=https://www.theverge.com/2021/4/29/22409501/feds-arrest-founder-bitcoin-mixer-laundered-cryptocurrency|access-date=2021-05-10|website=The Verge|language=en|archive-date=2021-12-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211229151419/https://www.theverge.com/2021/4/29/22409501/feds-arrest-founder-bitcoin-mixer-laundered-cryptocurrency|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-04-28|title=Individual Arrested and Charged with Operating Notorious Darknet Cryptocurrency "Mixer"|url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/individual-arrested-and-charged-operating-notorious-darknet-cryptocurrency-mixer|access-date=2021-05-10|website=www.justice.gov|language=en|archive-date=2021-12-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211220221831/https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/individual-arrested-and-charged-operating-notorious-darknet-cryptocurrency-mixer|url-status=live}}</ref> In March 2024 the verdict came back guilty on all counts. Roman's counsel plan to appeal the verdict. In November 2024, Sterlingov was sentenced to 150 months in prison. He was ordered to pay a forfeiture money judgment in the amount of $395,563,025.39, and forfeiture of seized cryptocurrencies and monetary assets valued at approximately $1.76 million. In addition, Roman was ordered to forfeit his interest in the Bitcoin Fog wallet, totaling approximately 1,345 bitcoin and currently valued at more than $103 million.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-08 |title=Operator of 'Bitcoin Fog' Sentenced to More Than 12 Years in Prison for Running Notorious Darknet Cryptocurrency Mixer |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-dc/pr/operator-bitcoin-fog-sentenced-more-12-years-prison-running-notorious-darknet |archive-url= |archive-date= |access-date=2024-12-13 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en}}</ref>

In 2022, the tumblers [[Blender.io]] and [[Tornado Cash]] were both sanctioned by the [[United States Department of the Treasury]], making it illegal for US citizens, residents and companies to use the service.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Clark |first=Mitchell |date=2022-05-06 |title=US punishes Blender.io for helping North Korea launder millions in stolen Axie crypto |url=https://www.theverge.com/2022/5/6/23060544/us-treasury-blender-io-sanctions-bitcoin-mixer |access-date=2022-08-08 |website=The Verge |language=en |archive-date=2022-06-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220609012528/https://www.theverge.com/2022/5/6/23060544/us-treasury-blender-io-sanctions-bitcoin-mixer |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Faife |first=Corin |date=2022-08-08 |title=US Treasury bans Tornado Cash mixer for role in crypto money laundering |url=https://www.theverge.com/2022/8/8/23296778/us-treasury-tornado-cash-crypto-mixer-sanctions-ethereum-north-korea |access-date=2022-08-08 |website=The Verge |language=en |archive-date=2022-08-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220808154359/https://www.theverge.com/2022/8/8/23296778/us-treasury-tornado-cash-crypto-mixer-sanctions-ethereum-north-korea |url-status=live }}</ref>

In March 2023, the tumbler [[ChipMixer]] and 46 million dollars in Bitcoin were seized.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Coote|first=Darryl|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/money/other/intl-operation-takes-down-chipmixer-money-laundering-service/ar-AA18HnDt|title=Int'l operation takes down ChipMixer money laundering service|agency=[[United Press International|UPI News]]|via=MSN|date=16 March 2023|access-date=1 April 2023|archive-date=17 March 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230317150305/https://www.msn.com/en-us/money/other/intl-operation-takes-down-chipmixer-money-laundering-service/ar-AA18HnDt|url-status=live}}</ref>

In April 2024, [[Keonne Rodriguez]] and [[William Lonergan Hill]], the founders of [[Samourai Wallet]], a privacy-focused Coinjoin tool that mixes a Bitcoin transaction with other transactions, were criminally charged by the [[United States Department of Justice|DOJ]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-05-09 |title=The government fears this privacy tool |url=https://reason.com/video/2024/05/09/the-government-fears-this-privacy-tool/ |access-date=2025-06-26 |website=Reason.com |language=en-US}}</ref> The DOJ alleged that providing these private, anonymous transactions enabled money laundering.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sun |first=Mengqi |date=2024-04-24 |title=Crypto Mixer Samourai Wallet's Co-founders Arrested for Money Laundering |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/crypto-mixer-samourai-wallets-co-founders-arrested-for-money-laundering-df237a4e |access-date=2025-06-26 |work=Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660}}</ref>

In late November 2025 German and Swiss authorities seized the servers of "cryptomixer.io", took the website down and confiscated some 25 million Euro in Crypto currencies. No arrests were announced but the contents of several mail accounts was secured. The operators are being investigated for money laundering.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-12-01 |title=Ermittler zerschlagen Plattform für Online-Geldwäsche|url=https://www.zeit.de/gesellschaft/2025-12/kryptowaehrung-behoerden-bundeskriminalamt-geldwaesche|access-date=2025-12-01 |website=Zeit.de |language=de}}</ref>
